analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $12 an hour and phases out the lower tipped wage.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and never received a vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $12 an hour in yearly steps, then adjust it automatically to keep pace with the median worker's pay. It would also raise the separate lower wage for tipped employees from $2.13 until it matches the regular minimum wage, and then eliminate the separate tipped minimum entirely. It requires employers to tell workers they have a right to keep their tips.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 15 million or more workers paid at or near the federal minimum, especially tipped workers such as restaurant servers, whose subminimum wage of $2.13 would eventually disappear. Workers in states where the minimum has stayed at $7.25 gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in yearly steps from $7.25 to $8, $9, $10, $11, and $12 an hour over four years [S2][S3].
After reaching $12, the wage is automatically adjusted each year to rise with the increase in the median hourly wage of all workers, so it no longer erodes with inflation [S2][S3].
Raises the tipped minimum wage from $2.13 toward the full minimum and then repeals the separate tipped wage entirely, so servers would be paid the same minimum as everyone else [S2][S3].
Requires employers to notify employees of their right to keep their tips, and states the right in statute [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage labor, concentrated in restaurants and other food service, retail, and personal care businesses, who face higher payroll costs; some of that cost could be passed to consumers through higher prices or absorbed through reduced hours and staffing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurant, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: The phased-in wage floor more than doubles the tipped minimum and raises the base minimum by about 65% over four years, a large and fast increase in labor costs for small restaurants and retailers that operate on thin margins; some businesses would respond with higher prices, reduced hours, or fewer staff [S2][S3].

The automatic index to the median wage locks in increases permanently without Congress voting again, which supporters see as protection against erosion and critics see as removing future elected judgment about the right level in a downturn [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are large and concentrated on people earning near the bottom of the wage scale: millions of workers would see direct pay raises, and tipped workers would move from a $2.13 base to the full minimum. The costs fall on the businesses that employ them, some of which would raise prices or trim hours. The five-year phase-in and the tip-credit transition soften but do not eliminate that adjustment. On balance this is a substantial redistribution from low-wage employers and their customers to low-wage workers, with genuine uncertainty about how many jobs would be affected at this magnitude.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day, and the committee took no further action before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on April 30, 2015, with 33 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction, and no further action is recorded in the bill's history [S5].
No markup, floor vote, or House counterpart action appears in the record before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage labor, including restaurant and retail operators, are better off because the bill died without a vote; they avoided the mandated wage increases. Low-wage workers, whose federal minimum remained $7.25 through 2017, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers; workers got no raise

sides.party_line_note: All 34 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Senate Republican supported it, and the chamber's Republican majority controlled the committee calendar and floor schedule.

industries.note: The bill phases out the $2.13 tipped minimum, which the industry relies on to shift a large share of server pay onto customers' tips, and raises the base wage that applies to kitchen staff. Its interest in blocking the bill runs directly against tipped and other low-wage workers' interest in the raise.
Retail, grocery, and personal-care businesses pay many workers at or near the federal minimum and would face step increases to $12, raising payroll costs or prices.
Workers at or near $7.25, and tipped workers especially, would receive direct, legally mandated pay increases, with the wage floor indexed to median wages thereafter.
